They are nigh perfect to play the opposing Stockmann brothers in Ibsen’s An Enemy of the People, now being given a zippy revival adapted by playwright Amy Herzog and directed by her husband, Sam Gold.

This brilliant Enemy of the People is notably funny in both its smarts and pacing, and even its later gathering darkness—when Stockmann is viciously trounced and isolated by his townsfolk—is studded with light, and the certainty of his self-preservation.
The actors are tremendous and completely lose themselves in the parts.
It’s the associations we make with these actors’ most famous roles that help complicate our understanding of the characters they are now portraying — and complicate what we take away from the play.
Director Sam Gold's production of An Enemy of the People skillfully balances the play’s history and its timeliness.
Herzog’s cracking adaptation runs just a little over two hours, with no official interval—only a 10-minute pause where you can go onstage and grab a (free) bracing shot of aquavit.
At times, it could use more vigour, but thanks to Strong’s presence this Enemy of the People is, deservedly, one of the season’s hottest tickets.
If you see An Enemy of the People—which, to be clear, you should—chances are that the disruptors will stay home for your performance.

What Ibsen never worried about is anyone calling his play “agitprop,” which is what Herzog and Gold have turned it into.

The spirit of morality, intolerance and the tensions that surround the brave act of whistle blowing live solid and true inside the new Broadway revival of An Enemy of the People , giving space to hidden greed and selfishness in the name of community and care.
Jeremy Strong offers a certain innocence in his performance that makes his journey all the more compelling.
This cast was fully committed in a way that was commendable and meaningful.
The fascinating but flawed Broadway revival also boasts star turns for two Emmy-winning actors, Jeremy Strong and Michael Imperioli, as the dueling Stockmann brothers.
As Stockmann, Strong is earnest and passionate and gives it as much energy as he can muster, but his performance feels flat.
And there is far too much editorializing as the narrative reaches its overly simplistic resolution.

cn.t: Critics praise Jeremy Strong's compelling performance and Amy Herzog's timely adaptation of Ibsen's classic, though some find Sam Gold's staging uneven or overly restrained, diminishing the play's dramatic power.

vs.sum: Broadway's only thrust-stage theater offers an unmatched intimate experience — no seat is more than a few rows from the action. Sightlines are excellent from every angle, though some seats face actors' backs during certain scenes.

acc.note: Elevator accessible through adjoining building. Loop technology and neck induction systems available.

vr.q: I find the play pretty riveting. And it's designed to make your blood boil and to make you think about the difficult ethical questions about our society that it poses.
Overall I thought it was great — it feels urgent, relevant, compelling — all things that a lot of great theater pieces do.
